# LDAP search filter built from HTTP request data (C#)

`qualor:csharp/ldap-injection` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-90](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/90.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A05:2025 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/), [A03:2021 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A03_2021-Injection/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data in ASP.NET Core (MVC and Web API controllers, Minimal APIs, Razor Pages) that
becomes part of the text of an LDAP search filter:

- `System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher`: the filter given to its constructors
  (`new DirectorySearcher(filter)`, `new DirectorySearcher(root, filter, ...)`) and its `Filter`
  property, set on a searcher variable, field or property or in an object initializer;
- `System.DirectoryServices.Protocols.SearchRequest`: the `ldapFilter` of its constructor and its
  `Filter` property.

The value is reported whether it is used as it is or built into the filter by concatenation,
string interpolation, `string.Format`, `string.Concat` or a `StringBuilder`. A value escaped with
`Encoder.LdapFilterEncode`, converted to a number, GUID or enum, or taken from a fixed allow-list
is not reported.

Request data means the parameters of controller actions, Razor Pages handlers and Minimal API
handlers (strings, string arrays, `StringValues`, forms, uploaded files, the body stream, and any
parameter bound with `[FromQuery]`, `[FromRoute]`, `[FromForm]`, `[FromHeader]`, `[FromBody]` or
`[AsParameters]`), `[BindProperty]` properties, and the request object itself (`Request.Query`,
`Form`, `Headers`, `Cookies`, `RouteValues`, `Body`, ...).
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
In an LDAP filter the characters `*`, `(`, `)` and `\` have a meaning of their own. A user name
such as `*` matches every entry, and one such as `admin)(|(objectClass=*)` adds conditions of the
attacker's choosing. Depending on how the result is used, this lets an attacker list the whole
directory, read attributes of other users, or pass a check that looks up a user and a password or
a group membership in the directory.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the name from the query string is put into the filter as it is.

```csharp
using System.DirectoryServices;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class PeopleController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult Find([FromQuery] string name)
    {
        using var searcher = new DirectorySearcher();
        searcher.Filter = "(&(objectClass=user)(cn=" + name + "))";
        return Ok(searcher.FindOne()?.Path);
    }
}
```

**Compliant:** the name is escaped for an LDAP filter before it is put into it.

```csharp
using System.DirectoryServices;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;

[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class PeopleController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult Find([FromQuery] string name)
    {
        using var searcher = new DirectorySearcher();
        searcher.Filter = "(&(objectClass=user)(cn=" + Encoder.LdapFilterEncode(name) + "))";
        return Ok(searcher.FindOne()?.Path);
    }
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Escape every value that goes into a filter as LDAP filter text: `*`, `(`, `)`, `\` and NUL
  must be written as `\2a`, `\28`, `\29`, `\5c` and `\00` (RFC 4515). The .NET AntiXSS `Encoder` class
  named by the OWASP LDAP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet does this with
  `Encoder.LdapFilterEncode`. Escaping for a distinguished name
  (`LdapDistinguishedNameEncode`) is not enough for a filter.
- Where the value can only be one of a few known values (an object class, a department), look it
  up in a fixed table instead of passing it on; where it is a number or an identifier, parse it
  first (`int.Parse`, `Guid.Parse`).
- Keep the filter's structure in your code: let the request supply values only, never parts of the
  filter such as attribute names or operators.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- ASP.NET Core MVC and Web API
- ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs
- ASP.NET Core Razor Pages
- System.DirectoryServices

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
Under `qualor dotnet end`, Qualor's Roslyn taint engine runs this rule in OpenGrep's place, on the
projects the build compiled. It follows request data across methods, files and projects, through
properties, expression-bodied members and services registered for dependency injection, and into the
code of compiled Razor views and pages (`.cshtml`), and it reads all C# the compiler accepts. A
finding is of high confidence, or medium ("Possible" in Qualor) when its path goes through data
stored earlier in the request, a lookup by a request key, or a call or view the engine could not
narrow down. The engine's own limits are listed in the [models' README](../../../models/README.md),
section "Known limits". The bullets below are the OpenGrep rule's: it runs outside
`qualor dotnet end`, on C# files no compiled project covers, and as the fallback when the engine
cannot finish.

- Taint is followed through the methods of one file, not into other files. Request data read
  inside an expression-bodied method (`=> ...`) or a property getter is missed.
- Minimal APIs: a class or record parameter bound from the JSON body without `[FromBody]` is not
  taken for request data, and a handler that is a method of another class is missed. A controller
  named `*Controller` whose base class has another name is missed.
- An enum parameter is reported when the enum is declared after its use or in another file. Only
  allow-lists written as `static readonly` tables of literals count; an equality check or
  `Enumerable.Contains(...)` called as a static method does not, and a variable assigned again
  after a check still counts as checked.
- Only the search filter is checked: request data in a distinguished name (a `DirectoryEntry`
  path, a search root, the base of a `SearchRequest`) is not reported. A search root created by a
  helper from request data is reported as if it were a filter when it is the only argument of
  `new DirectorySearcher(...)`, and so is an attribute list created by a helper from request data
  when it follows the filter.
- Only `Encoder.LdapFilterEncode` counts as escaping, recognised by that name: a class of your
  own named `Encoder` whose `LdapFilterEncode` does not escape is trusted all the same, while a
  hand-written escaper, or the method reached through another qualified class name, is still
  reported.
- `SearchRequest` is checked only as the type of `System.DirectoryServices.Protocols`, written out
  or imported in the same file; a file that gets that namespace from a global using is missed,
  and another library's `SearchRequest` declared in a file that also imports that namespace is
  reported when its `Filter` is set in an object initializer.
- OpenGrep 1.30 does not parse some newer C# syntax (raw strings with `$$"""`, types declared
  without a body such as `class X : Y;`, some multi-line collection expressions); code in those
  parts of a file may be missed.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/csharp/ldap/ldap-injection.cs`](../../../rules/csharp/ldap/ldap-injection.cs) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.
